rule: Everyday greetings beyond 'How are you?': 'How's it going?', 'How are you doing?', 'What's up?', 'Long time no see!', 'Good to see you!'. Answer naturally: 'Pretty good.', 'Not bad.', 'Can't complain.', 'Same as usual.', 'Busy as always!'. Reply back with 'And you?' or 'How about yourself?'.

examples.text: A: How's it going? B: Pretty good, thanks. You?
A: Long time no see! How have you been? B: I've been busy. How about you?

common_errors.error: A: How are you? B: Fine, thank you, and you?
common_errors.fix: A: How's it going? B: Pretty good, you?
common_errors.explanation: 'Fine, thank you, and you?' is a textbook template; native speakers mix it up naturally.

rule: Weather small talk starters: 'Nice day, isn't it?', 'It's freezing today!', 'It's pouring out there.', 'What's the weather like there?'. Use 'it' for weather: 'It's rainy', 'It's getting cold', 'It looks like rain'. Responses: 'Yeah, perfect for a walk.' / 'I know, I hate the heat.'

examples.text: It's so hot today. I'm melting!
A: It's pouring. Did you bring an umbrella? B: No, I'm soaked!

common_errors.explanation: Weather uses 'it' as the subject in English.

rule: Catching up with a friend: 'What have you been up to?', 'How's work going?', 'What did you do last weekend?', 'How was your day?'. Answer with past tense: 'I went...', 'I've been working a lot.', 'Nothing much, just stayed home.'.

examples.text: A: What have you been up to? B: Not much, just work and sleep.
A: How was your weekend? B: Great! I went hiking with friends.

common_errors.error: A: How was your weekend? B: I go shopping with my mother.
common_errors.fix: I went shopping with my mom.
common_errors.explanation: Recap of the past needs past tense (went), and 'go shopping' keeps no 'to'.

rule: Talking about work: 'What do you do?', 'I work in / I'm in marketing.', 'I work for a tech company.', 'I'm between jobs right now.', 'I work from home.', 'I have to work overtime today.' — note 'work for + company', 'work in + field'.

examples.text: A: What do you do? B: I work in finance, for a bank in Beijing.
I usually work from home on Fridays.

common_errors.error: What's your job? I am a worker of Tencent.
common_errors.fix: What do you do? I work for Tencent.
common_errors.explanation: 'What do you do?' is the natural question; say 'work for a company', not 'a worker of'.

rule: Describing daily routine with present simple + time words: 'I get up at seven, then I have breakfast and go to work.', 'I usually take the subway.', 'I have lunch at noon.', 'I get home around six.', 'I go to bed at eleven.' Add frequency adverbs: always / usually / sometimes / never.

examples.text: I usually get up at 6:30 and go for a run.
On weekends, I sleep in and hang out with friends.

common_errors.error: I get up at 7 o'clock, then I have my breakfast, then I go to work, then I...
common_errors.fix: I get up at seven. After breakfast, I head to work.
common_errors.explanation: Don't chain everything with 'then'; vary connectors like 'after', 'usually', 'later'.

rule: Talking about food: 'I'm allergic to peanuts.', 'I don't eat meat — I'm vegetarian.', 'I'm not a big fan of spicy food.', 'I have a sweet tooth.', 'It tastes amazing!', 'It's a bit too salty for me.'.

examples.text: I love Sichuan food, but it's a bit spicy for me.
Could I get this without garlic? I'm allergic.

common_errors.fix: I don't like eating spicy food.
common_errors.explanation: 'Like' takes a gerund (eating); 'spicy' needs a noun like 'food'.

rule: Talking about hobbies: 'What do you do in your free time?', 'I'm into photography.', 'I enjoy reading novels.', 'I play basketball twice a week.', 'I've been learning to cook lately.', 'I usually just watch TV and relax.'.

examples.text: A: What do you do for fun? B: I love hiking and taking photos.
I've been getting into yoga recently.

common_errors.fix: My hobby is playing basketball. / I play basketball.
common_errors.explanation: After 'is' use the gerund ('playing'), or just use the verb directly.

rule: Short natural answers make speech flow: Yeah / Uh-huh / Not really / Sort of / Kind of / You bet / No way / Totally / I guess so / I don't think so. Use them as replies to yes/no questions instead of full sentences.

examples.text: A: Did you like the movie? B: Yeah, it was great!
A: Are you tired? B: A little. / Not really.

common_errors.error: A: Are you free tomorrow? B: I am free. (stiff)
common_errors.fix: Yeah, I'm free. / Sure, I am.
common_errors.explanation: Full repeated sentences sound robotic; short answers are natural.

rule: Keep a conversation alive with listening responses: 'Oh really?', 'That's awesome!', 'Tell me more.', 'And then what happened?', 'Wow, that sounds fun!', 'I know, right?' — these signal you are listening and invite the speaker to continue.

examples.text: A: I went skydiving last weekend. B: No way! How was it?
A: I just got promoted. B: That's awesome! Congratulations!

common_errors.explanation: Active listening responses are expected in English conversations.

rule: Decline invitations softly: 'I'd love to, but I'm busy then.', 'Maybe another time!', 'Let me check my schedule and get back to you.', 'I can't make it tonight, sorry.', 'Next time for sure!' — always pair a refusal with a reason or an alternative.

examples.text: I'd love to join, but I have a family dinner that night.
Can't make it this week — how about next Tuesday?

common_errors.fix: I'd love to, but I can't this time.
common_errors.explanation: Bare 'no' sounds rude; soften with 'I'd love to, but...'.

rule: Expressing surprise: 'No way!', 'You're kidding!', 'Seriously?', 'What?!', 'That's unbelievable!', 'I can't believe it!', 'Are you serious?'. Intonation carries the emotion — raise the pitch.

examples.text: A: I won the lottery! B: No way! That's amazing!
A: She quit her job. B: Seriously? I can't believe it.

common_errors.explanation: Fixed exclamations sound far more natural than translating 'very surprised'.

rule: Vague language keeps talk casual: 'something like that', 'or something', 'and stuff', 'a bit', 'a couple of', 'roughly', 'more or less', 'kind of'. It sounds friendly, not sloppy — avoid only in formal writing.

examples.text: I'll be there around 6 or so.
We talked about work and stuff.

common_errors.error: I will arrive at 6:00 p.m. exactly. (too precise for casual)
common_errors.explanation: Casual plans use approximations; over-precision sounds robotic.

rule: Encouraging someone: 'You can do it!', 'Keep going!', 'Don't give up!', 'That's the way!', 'Nice try — you're almost there!', 'I believe in you!', 'Good luck! / Best of luck!'. Use them to motivate a friend mid-task.

examples.text: Come on, you've got this! One more rep!
Don't worry about the mistake — you're making great progress.

common_errors.explanation: Context decides: add encouragement words so it doesn't sound impatient.

rule: Safe small talk topics for daily practice: weather, weekend plans, food, travel, hobbies, family (general), current events (light). Starters: 'Have you tried the new café?', 'Did you watch the game last night?', 'Are you doing anything fun this weekend?'.

examples.text: Have you tried the new restaurant on the corner?
Are you doing anything fun this weekend?

common_errors.error: (Asking about salary or age with new acquaintances)
common_errors.fix: Stick to weather, plans, food, hobbies.
common_errors.explanation: Personal finance/age questions are taboo in casual English small talk.

rule: Giving a soft opinion in casual chat: 'I kind of like it.', 'I'm not really into sports.', 'It depends, honestly.', 'To be honest, I'd rather stay in.' — soften with 'kind of / not really / honestly' instead of stating opinions like facts.

examples.text: A: How do you like the new office? B: It's nice, though kind of far for me.
I'm not really into cooking, but I love eating out.

common_errors.explanation: 'Not really into' is the softer, natural everyday version.

rule: Winding down a chat naturally: 'It was great talking to you!', 'I've got to run — let's catch up soon.', 'Anyway, I should get going.', 'Let's talk again later!'. Always pair leaving with a warm closer so it doesn't feel abrupt.

examples.text: Anyway, I should get going — it was great talking to you!
I've got to run to a meeting. Let's catch up this weekend?

common_errors.fix: I've got to get going. Talk to you later!
common_errors.explanation: English pairs leaving with a natural closer phrase.

rule: Show interest while the other talks: 'Oh, that sounds fun!', 'Really? Tell me more.', 'Wow, how did that happen?', 'That's interesting — what made you try it?'. Asking one follow-up question keeps the friend-like rhythm.

examples.text: A: I started learning guitar. B: That's awesome! How's it going so far?
No way! Tell me more about the trip.

common_errors.explanation: Active reactions are the glue of casual English chat.
